_link.title: I can outline the effect of temperature on reaction rate using a Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution curve

toLevel2.stem: What does a Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution curve show?
toLevel2.answer: The spread of kinetic energies among particles
distractors: The activation energy of a chemical reaction
The concentration of reactants over time
The enthalpy change of a chemical reaction

toLevel2.stem: What happens to the Maxwell-Boltzmann curve at a higher temperature?
toLevel2.answer: It flattens and shifts to the right
distractors: It becomes taller and shifts to the left
It stays exactly the same shape
It disappears from the diagram

toLevel2.stem: On a Maxwell-Boltzmann curve, the area to the right of the Ea line represents:
toLevel2.answer: particles with enough energy to react
distractors: particles that have already reacted
the total energy of the system
the activation energy value

toLevel2.stem: At higher temperatures, the area to the right of the Ea line on a Maxwell-Boltzmann curve is:
distractors: smaller than at lower temperatures
the same as at lower temperatures
zero at all temperatures

toLevel2.stem: The x-axis of a Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution curve represents:
distractors: time elapsed in the reaction
concentration of the reactant
temperature of the system

toLevel2.stem: At a higher temperature, the Maxwell-Boltzmann curve flattens and shifts to the right, meaning more particles have higher kinetic energies.
distractors: False

toLevel2.stem: The area to the right of the activation energy line on a Maxwell-Boltzmann curve is smaller at higher temperatures.
distractors: True

toLevel3.stem: Why does a flattened, right-shifted Maxwell-Boltzmann curve at higher temperature lead to a faster rate?
toLevel3.answer: A greater proportion of particles now have energies exceeding Ea
distractors: The activation energy has been lowered by the temperature increase
The total number of particles has increased at higher temperature
The particles are oriented more correctly at higher temperature

toLevel3.stem: Why does the Maxwell-Boltzmann curve provide a useful way to explain the effect of temperature on rate?
toLevel3.answer: It visually shows the change in proportion of particles exceeding Ea
distractors: It measures the exact rate of the reaction at each temperature
It shows the concentration of products formed over time
It calculates the activation energy of the reaction precisely

toLevel3.stem: On a Maxwell-Boltzmann curve, why does the Ea line stay in the same position when temperature changes?
toLevel3.answer: Activation energy is a property of the reaction, not the temperature
distractors: The Ea always moves left when temperature is increased
The Ea always moves right when temperature is increased
The Ea disappears at high enough temperatures

toLevel3.stem: Why does even a small temperature increase cause a significant increase in the area beyond the Ea line?
toLevel3.answer: The Ea line is in the tail region where small curve shifts cause large area changes
distractors: Small temperature changes completely flatten the entire curve
The Ea line moves significantly to the left with any temperature change
Small temperature changes double the total number of particles

toLevel3.stem: What does the y-axis of a Maxwell-Boltzmann curve represent?
toLevel3.answer: The proportion of particles with a given kinetic energy
distractors: The total kinetic energy of all particles combined
The temperature of the particles at each point
The rate of reaction at each energy level

toLevel3.stem: Why is the curve always asymptotic to the x-axis on the right side, never touching it?
toLevel3.answer: There is always a small possibility of particles having very high kinetic energies
distractors: The curve must eventually reach zero when all particles have reacted
The x-axis represents concentration which cannot reach zero
The diagram is drawn incorrectly if it approaches the x-axis

toLevel3.stem: The activation energy line stays in the same position on a Maxwell-Boltzmann curve when temperature changes because Ea is a property of the reaction, not the temperature.
distractors: False

toLevel4.stem: A student draws Maxwell-Boltzmann curves at T₁ = 300 K and T₂ = 350 K. The Ea line is at 40 kJ mol⁻¹. At which temperature is the shaded area beyond Ea larger?
distractors: At T₁ = 300 K
Both have the same shaded area
Neither curve has any area beyond Ea

toLevel4.stem: A student draws a Maxwell-Boltzmann curve at 25°C and then draws a second curve at 50°C with the same peak height. What correction is needed?
toLevel4.answer: The 50°C curve should have a lower peak because it is broader
distractors: The 50°C curve should have a higher peak because it has more energy
Both curves should have the same peak height at any temperature
The 25°C curve should have a lower peak than the 50°C curve

toLevel4.stem: A student is asked to explain why a reaction rate doubles with a 10°C temperature increase. Using a Maxwell-Boltzmann curve, which explanation is correct?
toLevel4.answer: The slight rightward shift moves significantly more particles beyond the Ea in the tail region
distractors: The curve doubles in area, meaning twice as many particles exist
The Ea line shifts left by exactly the same amount as the curve shifts right
The curve becomes symmetrical at the higher temperature

toLevel4.stem: A student shades the area to the right of the Ea line on both a low-temperature and high-temperature Maxwell-Boltzmann curve. The high-temperature shaded area is much larger. What conclusion should they state?
toLevel4.answer: At higher temperature, a significantly greater proportion of particles exceed the activation energy
distractors: At higher temperature, the activation energy has been reduced significantly
At higher temperature, the total number of particles has increased dramatically
At higher temperature, the particles have been aligned more correctly

toLevel4.stem: A student is asked why food spoils faster in summer. Using a Maxwell-Boltzmann curve, which explanation is best?
toLevel4.answer: At higher summer temperatures, more particles exceed the Ea for decomposition reactions
distractors: Summer creates new bacteria that were not present in winter
The activation energy of decomposition reactions decreases in summer
Food contains more particles in summer than in winter

toLevel4.stem: A student draws two Maxwell-Boltzmann curves at different temperatures. They label the Ea line differently on each curve. What is wrong?
toLevel4.answer: The Ea line should be in the same position on both curves — it doesn't change with temperature
distractors: The Ea line should be at a lower energy on the high-temperature curve
Each temperature should have its own unique activation energy value
The Ea line should not appear on Maxwell-Boltzmann curves at all

toLevel4.stem: A student correctly draws two Maxwell-Boltzmann curves at T₁ and T₂ (T₂ > T₁) and notices that the T₂ curve starts at a higher point on the y-axis than T₁ near zero kinetic energy. Is this correct?
toLevel4.answer: No — both curves start at or near zero on the y-axis at zero kinetic energy
distractors: Yes — higher temperature means more particles at every energy level
Yes — the T₂ curve always starts higher because particles have more energy
No — the T₂ curve should start below the x-axis at zero kinetic energy

toLevel5.stem: A Maxwell-Boltzmann diagram shows that at T₁, only 5% of particles exceed Ea, but at T₂ (just 10°C higher), 10% exceed Ea. Analyze why such a small temperature change has such a large effect.
toLevel5.answer: The Ea line sits in the tail where the curve is steep, so a small shift greatly changes the area beyond it
distractors: The activation energy decreases by half when temperature rises by 10°C
The total number of particles doubles with every 10°C temperature increase
At T₂, all particles have exactly the same kinetic energy exceeding Ea

toLevel5.stem: A student claims: 'The Maxwell-Boltzmann curve shows that at high enough temperature, 100% of particles will exceed Ea.' Evaluate this claim.
toLevel5.answer: In principle yes, but the curve always has a tail near zero, so a tiny fraction always remains below Ea
distractors: Correct — at high temperature every particle has sufficient energy to react
Incorrect — temperature can never cause any particle to exceed Ea
Incorrect — only catalysts can make 100% of particles exceed Ea

toLevel5.stem: Two reactions have different activation energies. Reaction A has Ea = 30 kJ mol⁻¹ and Reaction B has Ea = 100 kJ mol⁻¹. For which reaction does a 10°C temperature increase have a greater proportional effect on rate?
toLevel5.answer: Reaction B — its Ea is further in the tail where the curve is more sensitive to shifts
distractors: Reaction A — its lower Ea means temperature has a greater effect
Both reactions show the same proportional increase with a 10°C rise
Neither reaction is affected by a 10°C temperature change

toLevel5.stem: A student argues: 'The Maxwell-Boltzmann curve is only useful for gases, not for reactions in solution.' Evaluate this claim.
toLevel5.answer: Incorrect — the distribution applies to particles in any phase at a given temperature
distractors: Correct — particles in solution do not have a distribution of kinetic energies
Correct — only gas particles can be represented on a Maxwell-Boltzmann curve
Incorrect — but the curve only applies to solutions, not gases

toLevel5.stem: A reaction has a very low Ea. On a Maxwell-Boltzmann diagram, most of the curve area is already to the right of the Ea line even at low temperature. What can be predicted about the effect of raising temperature?
toLevel5.answer: The rate will increase, but the proportional change will be smaller than for a high-Ea reaction
distractors: Temperature will have no effect because most particles can already react
Temperature will cause the rate to decrease because too many particles exceed Ea
Temperature will have a larger proportional effect than for a high-Ea reaction

toLevel5.stem: A peer says: 'At absolute zero (0 K), the Maxwell-Boltzmann curve would be a single spike at zero kinetic energy, meaning no reactions can occur.' Is this analysis reasonable?
toLevel5.answer: Yes — at 0 K all particles would have zero kinetic energy and no collisions could exceed Ea
distractors: No — particles always have some kinetic energy regardless of temperature
No — at 0 K the curve is broad and flat, showing a wide energy distribution
Yes — but reactions can still occur at 0 K through quantum tunnelling effects

toLevel5.stem: A student draws a Maxwell-Boltzmann curve at very high temperature. The curve is extremely flat with a very low peak. What does this indicate about the range of particle energies?
toLevel5.answer: Particles have a very wide range of energies with no single dominant energy value
distractors: All particles have the same very high kinetic energy at this temperature
Most particles have zero kinetic energy at extremely high temperatures
The curve indicates that no particles can exceed the activation energy

toLevel5.stem: A student suggests that Maxwell-Boltzmann curves could be used to predict the exact rate of a reaction at any temperature. Is this a valid use?
toLevel5.answer: Not exactly — the curve shows proportions, but the actual rate also depends on collision frequency and orientation
distractors: Yes — the curve gives exact rate values directly from the shaded area
No — Maxwell-Boltzmann curves have nothing to do with reaction rate
Yes — but only if the curve is drawn with perfectly accurate data points
